Ada yang hanya mengeluarkan asap dan abu tipis, ada pula yang meletus secara eksplosif dengan semburan material hingga belasan kilometer ke udara. Salah satu bahaya terbesar adalah awan panas, campuran gas dan material vulkanik bersuhu sangat tinggi yang meluncur cepat menuruni lereng. Setelah letusan, hujan deras dapat mengubah endapan abu menjadi aliran lahar yang merusak permukiman di lembah.

Manfaat bagi kehidupan

Meskipun berbahaya, gunung api juga membawa banyak manfaat. Abu vulkanik yang sudah melapuk membuat tanah sangat subur, sehingga lereng-lereng gunung menjadi kawasan pertanian yang produktif, misalnya untuk sayuran, kopi, dan teh. Panas bumi dari aktivitas vulkanik dimanfaatkan sebagai sumber energi untuk pembangkit listrik. Selain itu, pemandangan kawah, danau vulkanik, dan matahari terbit dari puncak gunung menarik banyak wisatawan setiap tahun.

Hidup berdampingan dengan gunung api

Masyarakat yang tinggal di sekitar gunung api telah lama mengembangkan pengetahuan lokal untuk membaca tanda-tanda alam, seperti perubahan suhu mata air, turunnya hewan dari hutan, atau bau belerang yang menyengat. Kini pengetahuan tersebut dilengkapi dengan sistem pemantauan modern. Lembaga pemerintah memantau aktivitas gunung api melalui alat pengukur gempa, pengamatan deformasi tanah, dan analisis gas. Status gunung api ditetapkan dalam beberapa tingkat, mulai dari normal hingga awas, dan setiap tingkat memiliki rekomendasi jarak aman.

Bagi warga dan wisatawan, penting untuk selalu memperhatikan informasi resmi, mematuhi larangan mendaki ketika status dinaikkan, dan mengetahui jalur evakuasi di daerah yang dikunjungi.

Allemansrätten – en frihet med ansvar

Den som har vandrat i de svenska skogarna har kanske förvånats över hur fritt man kan röra sig där. Det finns sällan staket eller skyltar som säger att man inte får gå vidare, och på en sommarpromenad kan man plocka blåbär, bada i en sjö eller slå sig ner på en klippa för att äta sin matsäck, utan att fråga någon om lov. Det beror på allemansrätten, en sedvana som ger alla människor möjlighet att vistas i naturen, även på mark som ägs av någon annan.

Allemansrätten är inte en vanlig lag med paragrafer som räknar upp vad man får och inte får göra. Den har vuxit fram ur gamla traditioner och nämns i grundlagen, men dess innehåll bygger till stor del på praxis och på principen om hänsyn. Den brukar sammanfattas med orden ”inte störa – inte förstöra”.

Vad får man göra?

Man får gå, cykla och rida i naturen, så länge man inte orsakar skada. Man får tälta en eller ett par nätter på samma plats, om det inte sker alltför nära ett bostadshus och om marken inte används för jordbruk. Man får plocka vilda bär, svamp och blommor som inte är fridlysta. Man får också bada och åka båt i sjöar och vattendrag, och tillfälligt lägga till vid en strand som inte ligger nära någons hus.

Vad får man inte göra?

Friheten har tydliga gränser. Man får inte gå över tomter eller trädgårdar, och man ska hålla avstånd till hus så att de som bor där kan känna sig ostörda. Man får inte gå på åkrar med växande gröda eller på planteringar där små träd kan skadas. Det är förbjudet att bryta kvistar eller fälla levande träd, och man får inte skräpa ner. Eldning kräver stor försiktighet och kan vara helt förbjuden under torra perioder, då brandrisken är hög. Hundar ska hållas kopplade under den period då många djur får ungar.

Varför fungerar det?

Att allemansrätten har kunnat leva kvar så länge hänger samman med ett ömsesidigt förtroende. Markägaren accepterar att andra rör sig på marken, och besökaren lovar i gengäld att inte lämna spår efter sig. När det förtroendet missbrukas, till exempel när stora grupper campar på samma plats eller lämnar sopor efter sig, uppstår konflikter. Därför diskuteras allemansrätten ofta, inte minst när antalet turister ökar och friluftslivet blir allt mer populärt.

För många svenskar är allemansrätten något självklart, nästan en del av den nationella identiteten. Den är en påminnelse om att naturen är något vi delar, och att friheten att njuta av den bara kan bevaras om var och en tar sitt ansvar. Den som lämnar en lägerplats i samma skick som den hittades bidrar till att även nästa besökare får uppleva samma tystnad och skönhet.

Zapomenutý deštník

Každé ráno v sedm hodin a dvanáct minut nastupoval pan Novák do tramvaje číslo devět. Sedal si vždy na stejné místo u okna, otevíral noviny a vystupoval přesně o osm zastávek později. Za třicet let, co jezdil do práce na úřad, se jeho trasa nezměnila ani jednou. Řidiči ho znali od vidění a stálí cestující si na něj zvykli jako na součást tramvaje.

Jednoho deštivého říjnového rána si pan Novák všiml, že na sedadle naproti leží zapomenutý deštník. Nebyl to obyčejný deštník. Měl dřevěnou rukojeť ve tvaru kachní hlavy a látku pokrytou drobnými žlutými hvězdičkami. Pan Novák se rozhlédl, ale nikdo se k deštníku nehlásil. Když dojel na svou zastávku, vzal ho s sebou s úmyslem odevzdat ho na ztrátách a nálezech.

Jenže v kanceláři přišla porada, pak telefonáty, pak hromada spisů, a deštník zůstal opřený v rohu. Večer s ním pan Novák odešel domů, protože pořád pršelo a jeho vlastní deštník ležel doma v předsíni.

Druhý den ráno si ho vzal znovu. A pak zase. Zjistil, že lidé v tramvaji se na něj usmívají. Malá holčička ukázala na kachní hlavu a zasmála se. Starší paní se ho zeptala, kde takový deštník koupil. Mladík se sluchátky na uších mu podržel dveře. Pan Novák, který s nikým v tramvaji za třicet let nepromluvil víc než pár slov, najednou zjistil, že se s lidmi baví.

Po týdnu ho však začalo trápit svědomí. Deštník přece někomu patří. Napsal tedy na kus papíru krátké oznámení – „Nalezen deštník s kachní hlavou, linka 9, ráno kolem sedmé“ – a připevnil ho na zastávce.

Za dva dny se ozvala mladá žena. Jmenovala se Klára a byla učitelka v mateřské škole. Deštník dostala od svých dětí ve třídě a byla smutná, že ho ztratila. Domluvili se, že si ho vyzvedne v tramvaji.

Když jí ho pan Novák podával, Klára se usmála a řekla: „Děti budou mít radost. Říkaly mi, že kachna určitě jen odletěla na výlet.“ Pak chvíli váhala a dodala: „Víte co? Jezdím touhle tramvají každý den. Můžeme si ho půjčovat. Když prší ráno, vezmu si ho já, když prší odpoledne, vy.“

Pan Novák se zasmál, poprvé po dlouhé době nahlas.

Od té doby měl každé ráno v tramvaji číslo devět s kým mluvit. Noviny zůstávaly častěji zavřené. A když se jednou za čas stalo, že pršelo celý den, sdíleli deštník se žlutými hvězdičkami cestou k zastávce oba.

A Balaton

A Balaton Közép-Európa legnagyobb tava, Magyarország egyik legismertebb természeti kincse és legkedveltebb üdülőhelye. A Dunántúlon, nagyjából délnyugat–északkeleti irányban húzódik, hossza mintegy hetvenhét kilométer, szélessége pedig néhány kilométertől körülbelül tizennégy kilométerig változik. Átlagos mélysége mindössze három méter körüli, ezért nyáron gyorsan felmelegszik, ami különösen vonzóvá teszi a fürdőzők számára.

Keletkezése

A tó geológiai értelemben viszonylag fiatal. Medre tektonikus mozgások következtében alakult ki, majd a mélyedésekben összegyűlt víz több kisebb tavat alkotott, amelyek idővel egyetlen összefüggő víztükörré olvadtak össze. Fő tápláló folyója a Zala, amely a nyugati végén, a Kis-Balatonon keresztül éri el a tavat. A Kis-Balaton mocsaras, nádas területe természetes szűrőként működik, megköti a folyó által hozott hordalék és tápanyagok egy részét, így hozzájárul a víz minőségének megőrzéséhez.

Két part, két arc

A Balaton északi és déli partja egészen eltérő jellegű. Az északi part dombos, vulkanikus eredetű hegyek szegélyezik, mint például a Badacsony vagy a Szent György-hegy. Ezeken a lejtőkön évszázadok óta szőlőt termesztenek, és a vidék híres borairól. A part mentén hangulatos falvak, régi présházak és templomok sorakoznak. A déli part ezzel szemben lapos, vize lassan mélyül, ezért különösen alkalmas a gyerekes családok számára. Itt találhatók a nagy üdülővárosok, strandok és szórakozóhelyek.

A Tihanyi-félsziget a tó északi partjáról nyúlik be mélyen a vízbe, és ott a tó a legkeskenyebb. A félsziget tetején álló apátság messziről látható, a környező táj pedig természetvédelmi terület.

Élővilág és időjárás

A Balaton vizében számos halfaj él, közülük a legismertebb a fogas, amely a magyar konyha egyik különlegessége. A nádasok fontos fészkelőhelyet biztosítanak a vízimadaraknak.

A tó felszíne időnként rendkívül gyorsan változik. Mivel sekély, egy hirtelen feltámadó szél percek alatt nagy hullámokat korbácsolhat. Ezért a parton viharjelző rendszer működik: a villogó fények figyelmeztetik a fürdőzőket és a vitorlázókat, hogy térjenek vissza a partra.

A tó vízminősége az elmúlt évtizedekben jelentősen javult. A szennyvízelvezetés korszerűsítése és a Kis-Balaton védelme nyomán a nyári algavirágzások ritkábbá váltak, és ma a fürdővíz legtöbbször tiszta, kellemes. A tó vízszintjét zsilipek szabályozzák, amelyek a Sió-csatornán keresztül engedik le a fölösleges vizet, aszályos években pedig igyekeznek visszatartani azt.

Turizmus

A Balaton a tizenkilencedik század óta népszerű üdülőhely. Nyáron fürdőzők, vitorlázók és kerékpárosok népesítik be a partokat; a tavat körülölelő kerékpárút különösen kedvelt. Kemény teleken a tó befagyhat, ilyenkor a jégen korcsolyázók és fakutyázók is megjelenhetnek, bár a jégre lépni csak a hivatalos tájékoztatás után, nagy körültekintéssel szabad.

Saunan hiljaisuus

Suomessa on arvioiden mukaan miljoonia saunoja, eli niitä on suunnilleen yhtä paljon kuin autoja. Sauna löytyy kerrostaloista, omakotitaloista, kesämökeiltä ja jopa toimistorakennuksista. Ulkomaalaiselle tämä voi kuulostaa liioittelulta, mutta suomalaiselle sauna on yhtä luonnollinen osa arkea kuin aamukahvi.

Saunominen on ennen kaikkea rauhoittumista. Lauteilla istuessa ei tarvitse olla tehokas eikä saavuttaa mitään. Puhelin jää pukuhuoneeseen, ja ainoat äänet ovat kiukaan sihahdus, kun löylyä heitetään, ja puun hiljainen ritinä. Monelle sauna onkin paikka, jossa ajatukset selkiytyvät ja päivän kiireet jäävät oven ulkopuolelle.

Saunan historia ulottuu satojen vuosien taakse. Vanhimmat saunat olivat savusaunoja, joissa ei ollut savupiippua. Kiuasta lämmitettiin tuntikausia, ja savu poistui pienestä aukosta seinässä. Kun lämmitys oli valmis, sauna tuuletettiin ja siitä tuli puhdas, lämmin tila. Savusaunaa pidettiin niin puhtaana paikkana, että siellä synnytettiin lapsia ja hoidettiin sairaita. Nykyään useimmissa kodeissa on sähkökiuas, mutta savusaunan pehmeää löylyä arvostetaan edelleen ja moni kesämökki ylpeilee omallaan.

Saunaan liittyy monia tapoja, jotka siirtyvät sukupolvelta toiselle. Kesällä saunasta mennään uimaan järveen tai mereen, ja talvella rohkeimmat pulahtavat avantoon tai kieriskelevät lumessa. Kesäisin saunassa käytetään vihtaa tai vastaa, eli koivunoksista sidottua kimppua, jolla taputellaan kevyesti ihoa. Koivunlehtien tuoksu kuuluu monen mielestä kesän parhaisiin asioihin. Saunan jälkeen istutaan kuistilla vilvoittelemassa, juodaan jotakin kylmää ja ehkä paistetaan makkaraa.

Saunaan liittyy myös sanaton etiketti. Löylyä heitetään niin, että kaikki lauteilla viihtyvät, ja on kohteliasta kysyä muilta ennen kuin heittää lisää. Jos löyly tuntuu liian kuumalta, voi aina siirtyä alemmalle lauteelle. Saunassa ei tarvitse puhua, ja yhteinen hiljaisuus koetaan pikemminkin mukavana kuin kiusallisena. Toisaalta moni tärkeä keskustelu on käyty juuri lauteilla, ja sanotaan, että saunassa kaikki ovat tasa-arvoisia.

Saunan terveysvaikutuksista keskustellaan paljon. Monet kokevat, että säännöllinen saunominen rentouttaa lihaksia, parantaa unta ja auttaa palautumaan rasituksesta. On kuitenkin hyvä muistaa juoda riittävästi vettä, välttää alkoholia saunoessa ja kuunnella omaa kehoa.

Saunasta kerrotaan myös paljon tarinoita. Vanhan kansanuskon mukaan saunassa asui saunatonttu, joka piti huolta tilasta ja rankaisi niitä, jotka käyttäytyivät huonosti. Siksi saunassa ei kiroiltu eikä riidelty, ja viimeiseksi saunaan jätettiin usein vähän lämmintä vettä tontulle. Vaikka harva enää uskoo tonttuihin, ajatus saunasta erityisenä, kunnioitusta ansaitsevana paikkana elää edelleen.

Suomalainen saunaperinne on hyväksytty myös kansainväliseen aineettoman kulttuuriperinnön luetteloon. Se kertoo, että sauna on enemmän kuin lämmin huone. Se on paikka, jossa puhdistetaan sekä keho että mieli, ja jossa ihmiset kohtaavat toisensa ilman kiirettä.

Margit Hollis had tuned pianos for thirty-one years, and in that time she had learned that a house tells you about its instrument long before you lift the lid. A house with radiators hissing under every window means cracked soundboards. A house where the curtains stay drawn all afternoon means felts eaten by moths. And a house like the one on Calloway Lane, with its gravel drive gone soft with moss and its porch light still burning at ten in the morning, usually meant that somebody had died and somebody else was trying to decide what to keep.

The woman who opened the door was perhaps forty, in a gray cardigan with the sleeves pushed up past her elbows. She introduced herself as Ruth and apologized for the boxes in the hall before Margit had said a word about them.

"It was my father's," Ruth said, leading her into a front room where the light came in slanted and dusty. "He played every evening. I don't think anyone has touched it since March."

The piano was an upright, dark walnut, with a music desk carved into a pattern of leaves. Margit set down her case, opened the top, and looked in at the hammers lined up like a row of patient birds. She pressed middle C and listened. Flat, as she expected, but not badly. The note had a warmth to it, a slight rounding at the end, that told her the old man had kept the room at a steady temperature and had not let the instrument suffer.

"Are you selling it?" she asked.

Ruth hesitated. "My brother thinks we should. He says nobody in the family plays." She ran a finger along the edge of the keyboard cover. "I took lessons when I was nine. I quit after a year. I was terrible."

Margit fitted the tuning hammer onto the first pin and began the slow work of setting the temperament. She did not use an electronic meter; she never had. She counted beats instead, the faint pulsing that two strings make when they are almost, but not quite, in agreement. A fourth should beat slowly, a fifth more slowly still. When the beats vanished entirely the interval was pure, but a piano could not be pure everywhere at once. The art was in distributing the small wrongness evenly, so that no key felt cheated.

Ruth sat on the arm of a sofa and watched. After a while she said, "He used to say that too. That every piano is a little bit wrong on purpose."

"He was right."

It took nearly two hours. When Margit finished she played a short scale, then a few chords, and then, because the room seemed to want it, a slow piece she had learned as a girl and never quite forgotten. The sound filled the space in a way it had not done when she arrived. Ruth had closed her eyes.

At the door, writing out the invoice, Margit said, "If you do decide to sell, call me. I know people who would treat it well."

Ruth took the paper and folded it twice. "I think I might take lessons again," she said. "Just to see."

Margit nodded and walked back down the soft gravel to her car. Behind her the porch light clicked off, and she did not turn around to see who had done it.

The alarm in Ring Four was not loud. Station designers had decided long ago that loud alarms caused more accidents than they prevented, so the warning that woke Teodor Vasquez-Lind at 0340 ship time was a soft, rising chime and a line of amber text across the ceiling of his bunk: HUMIDITY DEVIATION, GROWING BAY 4C.

He pulled on his coveralls and floated down the spoke corridor, catching handholds in the practiced rhythm of someone who had lived six years in rotating habitats and two in the zero-g hub. By the time he reached the bay the gravity had returned to its comfortable two-thirds, and he dropped onto the deck with a small grunt.

Anwen was already there, crouched beside the irrigation manifold with a diagnostic slate balanced on her knee.

"It's not a leak," she said without looking up. "I thought it was a leak. It's the condensers. Number three stopped cycling about forty minutes ago, and the others are trying to compensate."

Bay 4C held the station's wheat. Not all of it, but enough that a bad harvest would mean three months of ration adjustments and a great deal of complaining in the mess hall. The plants stood in long hydroponic troughs under violet lamps, their heads just beginning to fill. Teodor could feel the dampness on his face, heavier than it should have been.

"How high?"

"Eighty-four percent and climbing. Above ninety for more than a day and we start worrying about fungus."

He knelt beside her and opened the access panel on condenser three. The fault was obvious once he saw it: a coolant line had worked loose from its fitting, and a thin film of frost had grown across the coils where the refrigerant was escaping into the wrong chamber. The control system, seeing the temperature drop, had concluded that the condenser was overperforming and shut it down.

"It thinks it's doing too good a job," he said.

Anwen laughed, a short tired sound. "Story of my life."

The repair itself took twenty minutes. Teodor isolated the line, drained the stray coolant into a recovery canister, and reseated the fitting with a new seal from the spares locker. Anwen ran the condenser through a test cycle while he watched the pressure readings settle. Number three hummed back to life, and within a quarter hour the humidity display had begun its slow descent.

They sat together on an overturned supply crate and watched the numbers fall. Eighty-three. Eighty-two. Somewhere behind the troughs a ventilation fan changed pitch as the system adjusted.

"Do you ever think about how strange this is?" Anwen asked. "We're growing bread around a gas giant. My great-grandmother farmed potatoes in a field with a fence around it, and she thought the weather was the hardest thing in the world."

Teodor considered the violet light on the wheat, the faint curve of the deck rising away from them in both directions, the vast cold dark just beyond the hull.

"I think she was right," he said. "We just built our own weather. Now it's our fault when it breaks."

Anwen logged the repair, marked the fitting for inspection at the next maintenance window, and yawned. The humidity reached seventy-five percent as they left, and the wheat, which had never known any sky but this one, went on growing in the dark.

For most of my adult life I was not a morning person. I treated the hours before eight as a sort of hostile territory, something to be crossed quickly with coffee and the radio on loud. Then, three years ago, a dog came to live with me, and the dog had opinions about mornings that did not match mine.

Her name is Pepper. She is a mix of something low to the ground and something with a great deal of energy, and she wakes at a quarter to six with the regularity of a train timetable. At first I resented her for it. I would stumble out the door in whatever coat was nearest, eyes half shut, and drag us both around the block as quickly as possible. But dogs do not walk quickly when there are things to smell, and Pepper has always believed that there are things to smell everywhere.

So I slowed down, not because I wanted to but because I had no choice. And slowly, over weeks, I began to notice what the early morning actually looks like.

It looks, first of all, unfinished. The streetlights are still on but have lost their purpose, glowing faintly against a sky that is turning from charcoal to a pale washed blue. The houses are mostly dark. Here and there a kitchen window shows someone moving behind it, filling a kettle, and I feel an odd kinship with these strangers who are also awake before they need to be.

It sounds different, too. Without traffic, the neighborhood reveals a whole layer of noise I had never heard: the clatter of a recycling truck three streets away, the creak of a gate, a blackbird working through its long complicated song on the top of a chimney. In winter there is the scrape of someone clearing frost from a windshield. In summer there are sprinklers ticking on lawns.

I have come to know the regulars. There is the man in the green jacket who runs the same loop every day and always raises a hand without breaking stride. There is the older woman who walks two enormous gray dogs and talks to them in a steady, reasonable voice as though they were colleagues. There is the delivery van that parks outside the bakery at six-fifteen, its back doors open, trays of loaves passing from hand to hand in a cloud of warm air that I can smell from the corner.

None of these people know my name, and I do not know theirs. That seems right. The morning is a shared space without the obligations of daytime friendship. We nod, we pass, we go on.

I would like to say that this practice has made me a calmer, wiser person. I am not sure it has. I still dislike alarm clocks, and I still drink too much coffee. But I have noticed that on days when I walk early, the rest of the day feels less like something that is happening to me and more like something I have entered on purpose. I have already seen the light change. I have already heard the blackbird. Whatever comes next, I was there at the beginning.

Pepper, of course, takes no credit for any of this. She simply waits by the door each morning, tail going, as if to say that the world has been out there all along and it is about time I went to look at it.

HARLOW FERRY — The Millbrook Street Bridge reopened to traffic on Thursday morning, eleven months after floodwaters undermined its eastern pier and forced the closure of the town's main crossing over the Ossin River.

A small crowd gathered on both banks for the reopening, which began shortly after 9 a.m. with a ribbon cutting led by Mayor Delphine Achterberg and members of the county engineering department. A school brass band played from the western approach as the first vehicles, a mail truck followed by a line of cars and a farm tractor, rolled slowly across the deck.

"This bridge is more than concrete and steel," Achterberg told the gathering. "For almost a year, people in this town have been driving twenty minutes out of their way to get to work, to get their children to school, to visit family. Today that ends."

The bridge was closed last November after a week of heavy rain sent the Ossin to its highest level in more than four decades. Inspectors discovered that the current had scoured away much of the riverbed material supporting the eastern pier, leaving parts of its foundation exposed. Engineers judged the structure unsafe and closed it to all traffic within hours.

The repair project, which cost an estimated 6.4 million dollars, involved driving new steel piles into bedrock beneath the damaged pier, encasing the foundation in reinforced concrete, and placing a ring of heavy stone known as riprap around the base to protect it from future erosion. Crews also replaced the bridge's deck joints and resurfaced the roadway while the structure was closed.

County engineer Tomas Reyburn said the work had been complicated by high water during the spring, which halted construction for nearly six weeks.

"We had a narrow window in late summer when the river was low enough to work safely around the pier," Reyburn said. "The crews put in long days to make the most of it. I'm proud that we're opening ahead of the revised schedule."

During the closure, traffic between the two halves of the town was diverted to the Route 9 crossing roughly eight miles downstream. Local businesses on the eastern side of the river reported significant drops in customers. Several shop owners attended Thursday's ceremony.

"I think half of my regulars forgot I existed," said Ina Valcourt, who runs a hardware store two blocks from the bridge. "I'm hoping they'll remember now."

Officials said the bridge has been rated for full legal loads, including school buses and emergency vehicles. A temporary speed limit of 25 miles per hour will remain in effect for two weeks while crews complete minor finishing work on the sidewalks and railings.

The county has also announced plans to install a permanent river-level sensor on the bridge, which will send automatic alerts to the emergency management office when water rises above a set threshold. Reyburn said the sensor should be operational by early next year.

Asked whether residents should worry about future floods, Reyburn was cautious. "No bridge is immune to the river," he said. "But this one is in much better shape to handle a big flood than it was a year ago."

Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, lying between Irkutsk Oblast to the northwest and the Republic of Buryatia to the southeast. It is the deepest lake in the world, with a maximum depth of roughly 1,640 meters, and it is generally regarded as the oldest existing freshwater lake, with an estimated age of 25 to 30 million years. Because of its great depth, Baikal holds more water than any other freshwater lake on Earth, accounting for around a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water, even though several lakes exceed it in surface area.

Geography

The lake is long and narrow, shaped somewhat like a crescent, and stretches about 636 kilometers from southwest to northeast. Its width ranges up to roughly 80 kilometers, and its surface area is about 31,500 square kilometers. The surrounding landscape is mountainous, with ranges rising steeply from the shoreline on most sides. The largest island, Olkhon, lies near the western shore and is home to a small permanent population.

More than three hundred rivers and streams flow into Baikal. The most important is the Selenga, which enters from the southeast after draining a large area that includes part of northern Mongolia, and which forms a broad delta on the lake's shore. By contrast, the lake has only one outflow, the Angara River, which leaves Baikal at its southwestern end near the settlement of Listvyanka and eventually joins the Yenisei.

Geology

Baikal occupies a continental rift, a zone where the Earth's crust is slowly being pulled apart. The rift is still active, and the region experiences frequent small earthquakes. Beneath the water lies a thick layer of sediment, so that the floor of the underlying rift valley is several kilometers deeper than the lake bottom itself. Scientists believe the basin continues to widen by a few millimeters each year.

Climate and water

The lake lies in a region of harsh continental climate. In most years its surface freezes from about January until May, and the ice can become thick enough to support vehicles. The water is notably clear, and in some seasons visibility can extend to depths of several tens of meters. The deep waters are well oxygenated, which allows animal life to exist throughout the water column.

Ecology

Baikal's long isolation has produced an exceptional degree of endemism, meaning that many of the species living there are found nowhere else. Among the best known is the Baikal seal, or nerpa, one of the few seal species that live entirely in fresh water. The lake is also home to the omul, a fish of the salmon family that has long been important to local fisheries, and to a great diversity of small crustaceans, especially amphipods, which play a major role in keeping the water clean. Transparent oilfishes called golomyankas live in the deep zone.

Human history and protection

The shores of Baikal have been inhabited for thousands of years, and the lake holds cultural and spiritual significance for the Buryat people and other groups of the region. The Trans-Siberian Railway passes along its southern end. Concerns over industrial pollution, particularly from a pulp and paper mill on the southern shore that operated for several decades before closing in 2013, prompted long campaigns for its protection. In 1996 Lake Baikal was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The western honey bee (Apis mellifera) is a social insect that lives in large colonies and is kept by people around the world for honey, beeswax, and the pollination of crops. Native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia, it has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica.

Colony structure

A honey bee colony is made up of three kinds of adults. The queen is a single fertile female whose main role is to lay eggs. Workers are sterile or nearly sterile females that make up the vast majority of the colony, often numbering in the tens of thousands during summer. Drones are males whose primary function is to mate with queens from other colonies.

The sex of a bee is determined by a system known as haplodiploidy. Fertilized eggs develop into females, while unfertilized eggs develop into males. Whether a female larva becomes a worker or a queen depends on how she is fed. All young larvae receive royal jelly, a protein-rich secretion produced by glands in the heads of young workers, but larvae destined to become queens are fed it in abundance throughout their development and are raised in special enlarged cells.

During peak season a healthy queen may lay well over a thousand eggs per day. She mates early in life, during one or a few mating flights, and stores the sperm she receives for the rest of her life, which can last several years. Workers born in summer typically live only about five to six weeks, while those born in autumn can survive through the winter.

Division of labor

Workers perform different tasks as they age. Young workers usually stay inside the hive, cleaning cells, feeding larvae, building comb, and processing food. Older workers become foragers, leaving the hive to collect nectar, pollen, water, and plant resins. This progression is flexible, and colonies can shift the balance of tasks when conditions change.

Comb and food storage

Bees build their comb from wax secreted by glands on the underside of the worker abdomen. The comb consists of hexagonal cells, a shape that encloses a large volume for a given amount of wax. Cells are used to rear young and to store food. Nectar collected by foragers is passed to house bees, who reduce its water content and add enzymes, gradually converting it into honey, which is then sealed under a cap of wax.

Communication

Honey bees are well known for communicating the location of food sources through movement. A returning forager may perform a waggle dance on the comb, running in a straight line while vibrating her body and then circling back to repeat. The direction of the straight run relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle conveys distance. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch studied this behavior in detail and shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973 in part for this work. Bees also communicate extensively through chemical signals called pheromones.

Importance and threats

Honey bees pollinate a wide range of fruit, nut, and vegetable crops, making them economically significant far beyond the value of honey itself. In recent decades many beekeepers have reported increased colony losses. Contributing factors are thought to include parasites such as the Varroa mite, viral diseases, pesticide exposure, and poor nutrition resulting from reduced floral diversity.

The electrical telegraph was a system for sending messages over long distances by transmitting electrical signals along wires. Developed in the first half of the nineteenth century, it was the first technology to allow communication at speeds far faster than a person or vehicle could travel, and it reshaped commerce, journalism, warfare, and government.

Early development

Experiments with sending signals by electricity began in the late eighteenth century, but practical systems became possible only after advances in batteries and the discovery of electromagnetism in the 1820s. In Britain, William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle telegraph in 1837, in which electric currents deflected magnetic needles on a receiving panel to point at letters. Their system was adopted on several railway lines, where it helped coordinate train movements.

In the United States, Samuel Morse worked on a different design with the assistance of Alfred Vail and others. Their system used a single circuit and an electromagnet at the receiving end that could mark a moving strip of paper or produce audible clicks. Messages were encoded as sequences of short and long signals, which became known as Morse code. In 1844 a line between Washington and Baltimore carried a famous demonstration message, and within a few years telegraph lines were spreading rapidly across the country.

Technology

A basic telegraph circuit consisted of a battery, a key that the operator pressed to complete the circuit, a long wire strung on poles, and a receiving instrument. To reduce the cost of wire, many systems used the earth itself as the return path for the current. Over long distances signals weakened, so stations used relays, devices in which a weak incoming current operated a switch that controlled a fresh local battery, allowing the message to be passed along. Skilled operators soon learned to read messages by ear rather than from paper tape, greatly increasing speed.

Submarine cables

Connecting continents required laying insulated cables on the sea floor. Gutta-percha, a natural latex, proved to be an effective insulator for underwater use. The first transatlantic cable was completed in 1858, but it failed after only a few weeks of unreliable operation. A durable connection was established in 1866, with the large steamship Great Eastern playing a central role in laying the cable. By the end of the century a network of submarine cables linked much of the world.

Social and economic effects

The telegraph made it possible for news to travel across a continent in minutes rather than days. Newspapers formed cooperative arrangements to share telegraphed reports. Financial markets in distant cities became more closely linked, as prices could be compared almost instantly. Railways relied on the telegraph for scheduling and safety. Governments and armies used it to coordinate operations over great distances. The need for consistent timekeeping across telegraph and railway networks also contributed to the adoption of standardized time zones.

Decline

Over the twentieth century the telegraph was gradually displaced by the telephone, teleprinter networks, and later by electronic data communication. Telegram services nevertheless persisted for many decades. Western Union, long the dominant telegram company in the United States, ended its telegram service in 2006. The principles of the telegraph, including coded signaling, relaying, and networked communication, remain part of the foundation of modern telecommunications.

Northgate Precision Components
Unit 14, Fernhill Industrial Estate

17 October

Ms. Clara Ostrander
Purchasing Manager
Lindqvist Marine Systems

Dear Ms. Ostrander,

Re: Purchase Order 22-4471, machined pump housings

I am writing to inform you of a delay affecting the second delivery under the purchase order referenced above, to explain its cause, and to set out the steps we are taking to limit its impact on your production schedule.

As you know, the order covers 1,200 aluminum pump housings to be supplied in three equal deliveries. The first delivery of 400 units was dispatched on 2 October and, according to your receiving department, arrived in full and passed incoming inspection. The second delivery was scheduled to leave our facility on 24 October. I regret to say that we now expect to dispatch it on 4 November, eleven days later than agreed.

The delay results from a failure of the spindle drive on one of our two five-axis machining centers, which occurred on 12 October. The manufacturer's service engineer has confirmed that a replacement drive unit is required and that it will arrive at our facility no later than 21 October. In the meantime, we have moved the housing work to our remaining machining center and are running it on an extended shift pattern, including weekends. This has allowed us to keep production moving, but not at the full rate required to meet the original date.

We have considered whether to subcontract part of the work to another machine shop. After reviewing the tolerances specified in your drawing, particularly the bore concentricity and the surface finish on the sealing faces, we concluded that introducing a new supplier at this stage would create a greater risk to quality than the delay itself. I hope you will agree that this is the more responsible course, but I would be glad to discuss it further if you see the matter differently.

To reduce the impact on your assembly line, we propose the following:

First, we can make a partial shipment of 150 housings on 28 October, using units already completed and inspected. The remaining 250 would follow on 4 November.

Second, we will cover the additional freight cost of the split shipment in full.

Third, we will apply a credit of three percent against the invoice value of the second delivery in recognition of the inconvenience caused.

We remain confident that the third delivery will be dispatched on its original date of 21 November, as both machining centers will be fully operational well before work on it begins. I will confirm this to you in writing once the repaired machine has completed its first production run and passed our own acceptance checks.

Please let me know by 21 October whether the partial shipment arrangement suits your requirements, so that our logistics team can book the necessary transport. If another arrangement would serve you better, I am happy to consider it.

We value our relationship with Lindqvist Marine Systems and sincerely regret any disruption this delay may cause. Please do not hesitate to contact me directly should you have any questions.

Yours sincerely,

Gareth Mulholland
Operations Director
Northgate Precision Components

MEMORANDUM

To: All staff, Tessaline Analytics
From: Priya Venkataraman, Head of Operations
Date: 3 March
Subject: Changes to travel and expense procedures, effective 1 April

Over the past year the number of business trips taken by our staff has nearly doubled, reflecting the growth of our client base outside the region. This is good news, but it has also exposed weaknesses in the way we handle travel booking and expense claims. The finance team currently spends a disproportionate amount of time chasing missing receipts, correcting coding errors, and processing reimbursements that arrive months after the trip. Several of you have told us that the current process is confusing and slow. This memo sets out the changes we will introduce from 1 April.

1. Booking through the travel portal

All flights, rail travel, and hotel stays must be booked through the company travel portal unless there is a documented reason why this is not possible. The portal applies our negotiated rates automatically and records bookings directly against the correct project code. If you find a fare elsewhere that is substantially cheaper for the same itinerary, contact the operations desk before booking and we will either match it within the portal or approve an exception.

2. Submitting expenses

Expense claims must be submitted through the expenses application within thirty days of the end of the trip. Claims submitted after thirty days will still be processed, but will require approval from your department head. Each claim must include a photograph or scan of an itemized receipt for any individual expense above ten dollars. Card payment slips that do not list the items purchased are not sufficient.

3. Daily meal allowance

We are replacing the current system of reimbursing actual meal costs with a fixed daily allowance. The allowance will be set according to the destination city, using the rates listed on the operations page of the intranet. No receipts are needed for meals covered by the allowance. Where a meal is provided by a client or included in a conference fee, the corresponding portion of the allowance should be deducted.

4. Approval routing

Claims under five hundred dollars will be approved by your line manager. Claims above that amount will additionally be reviewed by the finance team. Our target is to reimburse approved claims within ten working days of submission.

5. Corporate cards

Staff who travel more than four times per year will be offered a corporate card. Use of the card for personal expenses is not permitted, even if you intend to repay the amount.

Training and support

The operations team will run two short online sessions demonstrating the travel portal and the expenses application: one on 18 March at 10:00 and one on 25 March at 15:00. Recordings will be posted on the intranet afterward. Attendance is strongly encouraged for anyone who travels regularly.

Questions

I recognize that changes to routine procedures can be frustrating, especially when they arrive in the middle of a busy quarter. Our aim is to make the process faster and less burdensome for everyone, including the finance team. If you have concerns about how these changes will affect your work, or suggestions for improving them, please contact me or Daniel Okafor in finance before the end of March. We will review the new procedures after three months and adjust them where necessary.

Thank you for your cooperation.

Review: Brightmill C40 Conical Burr Grinder

I have been grinding coffee by hand for about six years, first with a cheap ceramic grinder and later with a sturdier steel model, so I approached the Brightmill C40 with some skepticism. Electric grinders in this price range often promise consistency and deliver noise. After a month of daily use, I can say that the C40 mostly lives up to its claims, with a couple of caveats worth knowing before you buy.

Design and build

The C40 is compact, roughly the height of a large drinking glass, with a brushed metal body and a clear hopper on top that holds about 250 grams of beans. The grind setting is selected by turning a wide collar beneath the hopper, which clicks through forty numbered positions. The clicks are firm and well defined, which matters more than you might think: on some grinders it is easy to nudge the setting while refilling, and you only find out when your morning cup tastes wrong.

The catch container is made of a dense plastic with an anti-static coating. It works better than most. I still see a small amount of chaff clinging to the rim, but nothing like the clouds of fine powder I have dealt with elsewhere.

Grinding performance

The headline feature is the 40-millimeter conical steel burr set, and it shows. At the coarse end of the range, suitable for a French press, the particles are noticeably more even than those from my old hand grinder, with fewer fine fragments. At medium settings for drip and pour-over the results were consistent from day to day, and my brewing times became much more predictable.

At the fine end, the story is more mixed. The C40 can grind fine enough for espresso, but the steps between settings are slightly too large for precise adjustment. Moving one click changed my shot time by six or seven seconds, which is more than I would like. Dedicated espresso drinkers will probably want a grinder with stepless adjustment.

Noise and speed

The motor runs at a relatively low speed, which the manufacturer says reduces heat buildup. It also keeps the noise to a deep hum rather than a high whine. Grinding 18 grams for a pour-over took about twelve seconds. It is not silent, but I could run it early in the morning without waking anyone in the next room.

Cleaning and maintenance

The upper burr lifts out without tools after you remove the hopper, and a small brush is included. Cleaning took me about five minutes. I would have liked a little more guidance in the manual about how often to do it, but once a fortnight seems reasonable for daily use.

Shortcomings

Apart from the espresso limitation, my main complaint is the timer dial, which is only marked in rough increments and is not accurate enough to dose by time. I ended up weighing my beans before grinding, which is a habit I recommend anyway. The power cord is also rather short.

Verdict

For anyone brewing filter coffee, French press, or cold brew, the Brightmill C40 is an excellent choice that offers consistency usually found in more expensive machines. Espresso enthusiasts should look elsewhere. I am keeping mine, and my hand grinder has been retired to the camping box.

Rating: four out of five.

Field Test: Kestrel Ridge Trailmaster Mid Hiking Boots

When a pair of boots arrives promising to be "ready on day one," my instinct is to doubt it. Every pair of serious hiking boots I have owned has required at least a few weeks of breaking in, usually accompanied by blisters in new and creative places. So I was curious, and a little wary, when the Kestrel Ridge Trailmaster Mid showed up for testing. Over six weeks I wore them on roughly 140 kilometers of trail, ranging from dry gravel paths to wet, rocky ridgelines and one memorably muddy descent through a forest after two days of rain.

Fit and comfort

The Trailmaster is a mid-height boot with a leather and synthetic upper and a padded collar that wraps the ankle without pinching. I wear a standard width and found the fit true to size, with enough room in the toe box for my toes to spread on descents. The tongue is gusseted to keep out debris and is generously padded.

The claim about breaking in turned out to be largely accurate. I wore the boots straight out of the box on a twelve-kilometer walk and came home with no hot spots. By the end of the first week they had softened further around the flex point. I did develop one small blister on my left heel during a long, steep downhill section in the third week, but I suspect that had more to do with damp socks than with the boot.

Traction and support

The outsole uses deep, widely spaced lugs, and it performed well on loose surfaces and in mud, shedding clumps rather than clogging. On smooth wet rock the grip was good but not exceptional; I slipped once on a sloping slab beside a stream where I would have expected a softer rubber to hold. Torsional support is firm, and on uneven ground my ankles felt well protected without feeling locked in place.

Waterproofing and breathability

The boots use a waterproof membrane, and in my testing they kept my feet dry through several stream crossings at shin depth and a full day of steady rain. As is typical for membrane boots, they run warm. On a hot afternoon climb my feet were noticeably damp with sweat, and the boots took most of a night to dry out fully after a wet day.

Durability

After six weeks the uppers show some scuffing at the toe but no seam separation, and the lugs have worn only slightly. The laces, however, began to fray where they pass through the upper hooks, and I replaced them in week five. This is a small issue, but it is disappointing in a boot at this price.

Weight

At a little over 600 grams per boot in my size, the Trailmaster sits in the middle of its category. It is noticeably heavier than a trail runner but lighter than a traditional backpacking boot.

Conclusion

The Kestrel Ridge Trailmaster Mid is a comfortable, supportive, and genuinely waterproof boot that requires very little breaking in. Its grip on wet rock and the quality of its laces could be better, and hikers in hot climates may prefer something more breathable. For three-season hiking in changeable weather, though, it is an easy recommendation.

My grandmother's lemon cake was not a fancy thing. She baked it in a plain loaf tin that had gone dark and smooth with decades of use, and she never decorated it with anything more elaborate than a thin, crackling glaze. But on summer afternoons at her house it was always there on the counter under a glass dome, and I cannot smell lemon zest even now without seeing her kitchen: the yellow curtains, the radio murmuring about the weather, the back door open to the garden.

She never wrote the recipe down. When I finally asked her to teach me, she measured everything with the same chipped teacup and a soup spoon, and I had to stand beside her with a notebook converting her cups and spoonfuls into something I could repeat. What follows is my best attempt. It makes one loaf, enough for eight generous slices.

Ingredients

For the cake: 225 grams of plain flour, 2 teaspoons of baking powder, a pinch of salt, 175 grams of soft unsalted butter, 175 grams of caster sugar, 3 large eggs at room temperature, the finely grated zest of 2 lemons, and 100 milliliters of whole milk.

For the glaze: the juice of 2 lemons and 100 grams of granulated sugar.

Method

Heat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius, or 160 if your oven has a fan. Grease a standard loaf tin, roughly 23 by 13 centimeters, and line it with a strip of baking paper so that it overhangs the long sides. This makes lifting the cake out much easier later.

Sift the flour, baking powder, and salt together into a bowl and set it aside.

In a larger bowl, beat the butter and caster sugar together until the mixture is pale and fluffy. My grandmother did this with a wooden spoon and considerable patience. An electric mixer will do it in about three minutes. Add the lemon zest at this stage; rubbing it into the sugar with your fingertips first will release more of its fragrance.

Beat in the eggs one at a time, adding a spoonful of the flour mixture with the second and third eggs to stop the batter from curdling. Then fold in the remaining flour in two additions, alternating with the milk, until just combined. Do not overmix. The batter should drop easily from a spoon.

Scrape the batter into the tin, level the top, and bake for 45 to 55 minutes, until the cake is golden and a skewer inserted into the center comes out clean. If the top browns too quickly, cover it loosely with foil.

While the cake bakes, stir the lemon juice and granulated sugar together in a small bowl. Do not try to dissolve the sugar completely. The undissolved crystals are what give the glaze its crunch.

As soon as the cake comes out of the oven, prick it all over with a skewer, going deep, and spoon the lemon syrup slowly over the top, letting it soak in. Leave the cake in its tin until completely cool. As it cools, the sugar sets into a thin, crisp crust.

Serving

My grandmother served it in thick slices with nothing else, and I have never found a reason to improve on that. Kept in an airtight tin, it stays moist for three or four days, and I think it tastes even better on the second day, when the lemon has had time to settle into every crumb.

Lisbon: An Introduction for Visitors

Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, spreads across a series of steep hills on the northern bank of the Tagus River, close to where it widens into a broad estuary before meeting the Atlantic Ocean. It is one of the oldest cities in western Europe, and its long history as a port and the center of a seafaring empire is visible everywhere, from its riverside monuments to its tiled facades. The city is compact enough to explore on foot, provided you are willing to climb.

Getting around

Lisbon's hills are the first thing most visitors notice. Comfortable shoes with good grip are essential, as many streets and squares are paved with small, polished limestone and basalt cobbles arranged in decorative patterns, which can be slippery when wet. The city has a metro system, buses, and several historic trams. Tram 28 is famous for its winding route through the older districts and is often crowded with visitors; riding it early in the morning is usually more pleasant. Several funiculars and a historic street elevator, the Santa Justa Lift, help connect the lower town with the higher neighborhoods.

Baixa and the 1755 earthquake

The central lower district, the Baixa, was largely rebuilt after a catastrophic earthquake in 1755, which was followed by a tsunami and widespread fires. Under the direction of the Marquis of Pombal, the area was reconstructed on a regular grid of streets with buildings designed to resist future tremors. At its riverside edge lies the grand Praça do Comércio, a large square open to the water on one side and framed by arcaded buildings on the other three.

Alfama and the castle

East of the Baixa, the Alfama district climbs the hill toward the Castle of São Jorge. Alfama survived the earthquake comparatively well, and its narrow lanes, stairways, and small squares preserve an older street pattern. The castle walls offer wide views across the city and river. Along the way, several miradouros, or viewpoints, provide places to rest and look out over the terracotta rooftops.

Bairro Alto and Chiado

To the west, Chiado is known for its cafes, bookshops, and theaters, while the neighboring Bairro Alto is quiet by day and busy with small bars and restaurants at night. Both are good areas to hear fado, the melancholy traditional song form closely associated with Lisbon, which was inscribed by UNESCO on its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.

Belém

A few kilometers west along the river, the Belém district contains some of Lisbon's best-known monuments. The Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower, both built in the early sixteenth century in the ornate style known as Manueline, are together listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Nearby stands the Monument to the Discoveries, a large twentieth-century sculpture honoring Portuguese navigators. Belém is also the traditional home of pastéis de nata, the custard tarts with crisp pastry that are now sold throughout the city.

Practical notes

Summers are hot and dry, while winters are mild but can be rainy. Spring and autumn are generally the most comfortable seasons for walking. Many museums close on Mondays, so check opening times before planning your day. Finally, take time simply to wander: some of Lisbon's most memorable moments come from turning into an unfamiliar street and finding a view of the river at the bottom of it.

Elm Hollow Community Garden Association
Minutes of the Monthly General Meeting
Held in the meeting room of the Elm Hollow Branch Library

Present: Joan Fairweather (Chair), Malik Henshaw (Treasurer), Lucia Ferreira (Secretary), and fourteen members. Apologies were received from Bernard Ilves and Sunita Rao.

1. Opening

The Chair opened the meeting at 7:05 p.m. and welcomed two new members, Ethan Dowd and Mariela Cruz, who were allocated plots 23 and 31 in September.

2. Minutes of the previous meeting

The minutes of the August meeting were approved without amendment. Proposed by Malik Henshaw, seconded by Rosa Lindgren.

3. Matters arising

The Chair reported that the broken hinge on the main gate had been replaced by a volunteer, as agreed at the last meeting. The replacement cost twenty-two dollars, which has been reimbursed from the maintenance fund.

The Secretary confirmed that she had written to the city parks department about the overhanging branches from the adjacent lot. A reply has not yet been received. Action: the Secretary will follow up by telephone before the next meeting.

4. Treasurer's report

The Treasurer reported a current balance of 1,486 dollars. Income since the last meeting consisted of plot fees from the two new members and 140 dollars from the plant sale held on 9 September. Expenses included the gate hinge, a replacement hose, and the annual insurance renewal of 310 dollars. The Treasurer noted that three members have not yet paid their annual fees and will receive a reminder letter.

5. Water supply

Several members raised concerns about low water pressure at the eastern end of the garden during the dry weeks of August. Discussion followed. Tom Abernathy suggested that the problem was caused by too many hoses being used at once in the evening. Others suggested that the main supply line might be partly blocked.

It was agreed that a rota for evening watering would be trialed next summer, and that the committee would ask a plumber to inspect the supply line before the ground freezes. The Treasurer advised that up to 200 dollars could be spent on the inspection without affecting other planned expenses.

Motion: to authorize the committee to spend up to 200 dollars on an inspection of the water supply line. Proposed by Rosa Lindgren, seconded by Ethan Dowd. Carried unanimously.

6. Compost area

The Chair reported that the compost bins had again been contaminated with plastic plant pots and food packaging. Members were reminded that only plant material from the garden should be added. Lucia Ferreira offered to make new laminated signs for the bins.

7. Autumn workday

The autumn workday will be held on Saturday, 21 October, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tasks will include clearing the shared herb bed, spreading wood chips on the main paths, and storing the communal tools for winter. Members were asked to sign up on the sheet circulated during the meeting. Light refreshments will be provided.

8. Any other business

Mariela Cruz asked whether the association had considered starting a seed library. Several members expressed interest. The Chair invited Ms. Cruz to bring a short written proposal to the November meeting.

9. Date of next meeting

The next general meeting will be held on Tuesday, 14 November, at 7 p.m. in the same location.

The meeting closed at 8:20 p.m.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you all for coming.

When the committee asked me to say a few words tonight, I agreed immediately, and then spent three weeks wondering how anyone could possibly sum up twenty-eight years of Evelyn Marchetti in a short speech. I have decided that it cannot be done, so instead I am going to tell you a few things I know about her, and trust that the rest of you will fill in the gaps over dessert.

Evelyn arrived at Westbrook Secondary School as its librarian at a time when the library was, to put it kindly, an afterthought. It was a long, narrow room at the end of the science corridor, with shelves that sagged in the middle and a collection that had not been seriously updated since before most of our current students' parents were born. There was a sign on the door listing eleven rules, nine of which began with the word "no."

The first thing Evelyn did, so the story goes, was take down that sign. The second thing she did was put a kettle in the back office. And the third thing she did was start learning the names of every student who walked through the door.

I was one of those students. I was fourteen, I was new to the school, and I did not have many friends. I spent most lunchtimes in the library because it was quiet and nobody asked me questions. After about a week, Evelyn walked over to the table where I was sitting, put a book down in front of me, and said, "I think you might like this one. If you don't, bring it back and tell me why." Then she walked away.

I did like it. And when I brought it back, she asked me what I thought, and actually listened to the answer, and then handed me another one. That went on for four years. I am not exaggerating when I say that I became a teacher partly because of that table in the corner and the steady stream of books that arrived on it.

I know I am not the only one. Over the past month, as we prepared for this evening, we invited former students to send in messages. We received more than three hundred. They came from nurses and engineers, from carpenters and poets, from people who now live on the other side of the world. Many of them said some version of the same thing: that the library was the place where they first felt that they belonged somewhere.

Of course, Evelyn did much more than recommend books. She fought, year after year, for budgets that were never quite large enough. She turned that narrow room into a place with computers, study spaces, a reading club, a chess club, and, at one point, a rather ambitious tank of tropical fish that we will not discuss further. She trained a generation of student volunteers. She was the first to arrive at open evenings and the last to leave.

Evelyn, you have told us that you plan to spend your retirement traveling, gardening, and, in your words, "finally reading something without wondering whether a fifteen-year-old would like it." You have earned every minute of it.

On behalf of the staff, the students, past and present, and everyone in this room, thank you. Please raise your glasses to Evelyn Marchetti.

How to Repair a Punctured Bicycle Inner Tube

A flat tire is the most common mechanical problem cyclists face, and fixing one at the roadside is a skill worth learning. With a few inexpensive tools and some practice, the whole job takes about fifteen minutes.

What you will need

A patch kit containing patches, a small tube of vulcanizing solution or self-adhesive patches, and a piece of sandpaper. Two or three plastic tire levers. A pump that fits your valve type. Optionally, a spare inner tube, which lets you get moving quickly and repair the punctured tube at home.

Step 1: Remove the wheel

Shift the chain onto the smallest rear sprocket if you are working on the rear wheel; this makes removal and refitting easier. Release the brake if your bike has rim brakes, then open the quick-release lever or loosen the axle nuts and take the wheel out of the frame.

Step 2: Remove the tire from the rim

Let out any remaining air. Push the valve up into the tire slightly. Insert a tire lever under the edge of the tire, called the bead, opposite the valve, and pry it over the rim wall. Hook the lever onto a spoke. Insert a second lever a few centimeters away and do the same, then slide it around the rim until one side of the tire comes free. Pull the inner tube out, finishing at the valve.

Step 3: Find the puncture

Pump some air into the tube and listen for the hiss. Passing the tube close to your cheek or lips can help, as you will feel escaping air. If you still cannot find the hole, submerge sections of the tube in a bowl of water and watch for bubbles. Mark the hole with a pen or by keeping your thumb on it.

Step 4: Find the cause

This step is often skipped, and it is the reason many repairs fail within minutes. Carefully run your fingers around the inside of the tire to find whatever caused the puncture, such as a thorn, a shard of glass, or a piece of wire. Remove it. Line up the position of the hole in the tube with the tire to help locate the culprit. Also check that the rim tape covers all the spoke holes.

Step 5: Patch the tube

Let the air out. Roughen an area slightly larger than the patch around the hole with sandpaper. If using vulcanizing solution, spread a thin layer over the roughened area and wait until it becomes dull and tacky, usually a few minutes. Peel the backing from the patch and press it firmly onto the tube, working from the center outward. Hold it under firm pressure for at least a minute.

Step 6: Refit the tube and tire

Inflate the tube just enough to give it shape. Insert the valve through the rim hole, then tuck the tube into the tire all the way around. Starting at the valve, push the tire bead back over the rim with your thumbs, working around both sides toward the point opposite the valve. The last section will be tight. Try to finish with your hands rather than levers, which can pinch the tube.

Step 7: Inflate and check

Before inflating fully, inspect both sides of the tire to make sure the tube is not caught between the bead and the rim. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Refit the wheel, reconnect the brake, and spin the wheel to check that it runs true.

The garage door stuck halfway, the way it always had, and Nadia had to duck under it with the box of trash bags held against her chest. Inside, the air smelled of motor oil and old cardboard. Her brother was already standing in the middle of the concrete floor, looking at the shelves as if they might attack him.

"Where do we even start?" Owen said.

"Left wall. We go left to right. Keep, donate, throw."

"You made a system."

"Someone had to make a system." She dropped the box and pulled out three bags. "Mum kept everything, Owen. If we don't have a system we'll be here until Christmas."

He picked up a paint tin from the lowest shelf and shook it. Something solid rattled inside. "What do you think this was?"

"Throw."

"You didn't even look at it."

"It's a paint tin from nineteen ninety-something with a rock in it. Throw."

He dropped it into the bag. For a while they worked without talking. Garden tools, mostly rusted. A box of jam jars. A broken lamp. A set of encyclopedias with the spines faded to the color of weak tea. Nadia put those in the donate pile, then hesitated, then took one back out and flipped through it.

"Remember when you used these for every school project?" she said.

"I copied a whole page about volcanoes once. Word for word. Mr. Adeyemi gave me a C and wrote 'whose words are these' in red pen across the top."

"Serves you right."

"I was nine." He reached up to the top shelf and pulled down a long, flat box. "Hang on. Nadia. Look."

It was the board game. The one with the little plastic boats and the map of islands, the one they had played every rainy weekend until the spinner broke and their father fixed it with a paper clip. Owen opened the lid. The paper clip was still there.

"I can't believe she kept this," Nadia said.

"I can. She kept the paint tin with the rock in it."

She laughed, and then, unexpectedly, her eyes stung. She looked away at the window, where a spider had built an elaborate web across one corner.

"Do you want it?" Owen asked quietly.

"I don't know. Do you?"

"I don't have anyone to play it with."

"You have me."

He looked at her for a moment. "You always cheated."

"I did not."

"You moved your boat when you thought I wasn't looking. Every single time."

"That was a legitimate strategy."

"That was cheating, Nadia."

She took the box from him and put it carefully on the bonnet of the old car, away from all three piles. "Keep," she said. "We'll argue about it later."

"We'll argue about it at Christmas."

"Probably."

He nodded, and turned back to the shelves, and reached for the next box. It was labeled, in their mother's neat, slanted handwriting, simply: Things That Might Be Useful. Owen held it up so his sister could see.

"Oh no," Nadia said, and they both started laughing, and for a minute neither of them could stop.

Five Weathers

I. Fog

The street forgets itself by seven.
Lamp posts stand like questions
nobody remembers asking.
A cyclist rings his bell at nothing
and the nothing answers,
soft, gray, close enough to touch,
holding the whole town in its open hand
as if it had not decided yet
what to do with us.

II. Heat

All afternoon the tar remembers sun.
Dogs lie flat as dropped coats in doorway shade.
The ice in my glass gives up
one small surrender at a time,
and the radio, half asleep,
reads out the names of towns
where it is cooler,
places I have never been
and suddenly wish to visit
only for their temperatures.

III. First Snow

My daughter presses her whole face
to the cold kitchen window
and does not speak, which is rare.
Outside, the garden is being rewritten
in a language with no hard edges.
The bird feeder wears a small white hat.
Later she will want boots, mittens, a sled,
noise, but for now there is only this:
two of us breathing on the glass,
and the world arriving slowly,
one weightless piece after another.

IV. Wind

It came through the night
like a rumor no one could stop,
rattling gates, lifting a neighbor's
trash lid and carrying it three doors down,
pulling at the loose gutter
with the patience of a creditor.
In the morning the sky was scrubbed bright,
the street full of leaves
arranged in no order at all,
and everyone came out to look
at what had been moved,
and what, against all likelihood,
had stayed.

V. Rain After a Long Dry Month

At first we did not believe it.
A few dark coins on the pavement,
then more, then the whole sky
letting go of something it had carried too long.
The smell rose from the ground,
mineral and green,
older than any of us.
My neighbor stood bareheaded in her yard,
palms up, face up,
laughing like someone handed back
a thing she had not known was missing.
I stood in my doorway and did not go in.
The gutters began to sing.
The garden drank and drank.

Coda

Each day a different sky
leans down to tell us
we are not in charge.
I have stopped arguing.
I keep an umbrella by the door,
a hat on the hook,
a window clean enough to see through,
and I let the weather
do what it has always done:
change its mind, and change mine.

The ledger went missing on a Tuesday, between the 4:40 crossing and the 5:15, and by the time Inspector Halloran arrived at the ferry terminal the harbor master had already accused three people and apologized to two of them.

"It was right here," said Cormac Dunleavy, tapping the empty space on his desk with a thick forefinger. "Leather cover, green. The full manifest records for the season. I stepped out to deal with a lorry that had parked across the loading lane, and when I came back it was gone."

Halloran looked around the small office. One door to the waiting hall, one window facing the quay, a filing cabinet, a kettle, a calendar from a marine supply company showing a lighthouse. The window was latched from the inside.

"How long were you out?"

"Ten minutes. Maybe twelve."

"Who knew the ledger was here?"

Dunleavy spread his hands. "Anyone who works the terminal. The ticket clerk, Siobhan. Both deckhands. The woman who runs the cafe. Half the regular drivers, probably. It's not a secret where I keep it."

"And why would anyone want it?"

The harbor master's face closed slightly. "I've no idea."

Halloran made a note of that, and of the way Dunleavy's eyes had moved, for just a moment, toward the filing cabinet.

She interviewed the ticket clerk first. Siobhan Garvey was young and nervous and remembered seeing nobody go into the office, but admitted that she had been on the telephone for much of the time arguing with a customer about a refund. The cafe owner had been serving a coach party. One deckhand had been on the vessel. The other, a broad, quiet man named Piotr, had been helping to move the lorry.

"Who parked the lorry?" Halloran asked him.

Piotr frowned. "That was strange. Driver said he'd been told to wait there. By phone. But he didn't know who had called him."

Halloran walked back to the office slowly. A lorry deliberately placed to block the lane. A harbor master called outside at a predictable moment. Someone who knew exactly how long he would be gone.

And a man who did not want to say why anyone might want his records.

She found Dunleavy staring out at the gray water. "Mr. Dunleavy," she said, "I think whoever took your ledger didn't want to steal it. I think they wanted to read it, and they needed you away from your desk to do it."

He said nothing.

"So the question isn't who took it. The question is what's in it. And I think you know."

For a long moment the only sound was the slap of water against the pilings. Then Dunleavy sighed, opened the filing cabinet, and took out a second notebook, smaller, with a plain brown cover.

"The green ledger is what goes to the port authority," he said. "This one is what actually crossed."

Halloran held out her hand for it. Outside, the 5:50 ferry sounded its horn, and somewhere on the far side of the water, she suspected, a person was reading a set of numbers and slowly realizing they did not add up.

In the city of Orvell, where the streets rearranged themselves a little every spring, the mapmakers were the most important people after the bakers.

Lira had been apprenticed to Master Tobin Ashgrove for three years, and in that time she had learned to grind ink from oak galls, to stretch vellum without tearing it, and to walk a street with her eyes half closed so that she could feel the faint pull where it was beginning to drift. What she had not yet been allowed to do was draw a map of her own.

"Not until you can hear the city," Tobin said, whenever she asked.

"Hear it saying what?"

"Whatever it's saying." And he would go back to his work, bent over the great table under the north window, his pen moving across the parchment in small, certain strokes.

Then, in the third week of the thaw, Tobin fell ill. It was nothing serious, the physician said, only a fever that needed rest, but it came at the worst possible time. Every spring the guild issued new maps of the eastern quarter, where the drift was strongest, and every merchant, carter, and lamplighter in Orvell relied on them. Without new maps, people would turn familiar corners and find themselves in alleys that had not been there the week before.

"You'll have to do it," Tobin said from his bed, his voice hoarse. "The eastern quarter. Start at the Bellwater fountain and work outward."

Lira stared at him. "I can't. I haven't heard anything."

"You've been hearing it for months. You just haven't been listening."

She set out at dawn with a satchel of blank sheets, a lead stylus, and a pocket compass that, like all compasses in Orvell, was useful only for telling her which way the wind was blowing. The Bellwater fountain was where it had always been; fountains rarely moved. But the street beyond it, which last year had run straight toward the river, now bent gently to the left, and halfway along it a narrow lane had opened between two houses where before there had been a wall.

She stood at the mouth of the new lane and closed her eyes, the way Tobin had taught her.

At first there was only the ordinary noise of morning: shutters opening, a cart on the cobbles, a bird somewhere above. Then, beneath it, she noticed something else. A kind of low hum, almost below hearing, that rose slightly when she faced one direction and fell when she faced another. It was not a sound exactly. It was more like the feeling of a song she had almost forgotten.

The street wanted to go toward the old market. It had not got there yet, but it was trying.

Lira opened her eyes, pressed a sheet of vellum against the wall, and began to draw. She drew the bend, and the new lane, and then, very lightly, a dotted line showing where she thought the street would be by midsummer.

When she brought the sheets home that evening, Tobin looked at them for a long time without speaking. At last he pointed at the dotted line.

"Who taught you to do that?"

"Nobody," she said. "The street told me."

He smiled, and handed the sheets back to her. "Then you're a mapmaker," he said, and closed his eyes to sleep.

GREYSTONE VALLEY — Researchers surveying a remote section of the Carrow Highlands Nature Reserve have identified a previously undescribed species of ground beetle, according to a paper published this week in a regional journal of entomology.

The beetle, which has been given the scientific name Carabus carrowensis, is about 22 millimeters long, with a dark metallic body that shows a faint copper sheen under strong light. The research team found it in a narrow band of mossy boulder fields above the tree line, at altitudes between roughly 1,100 and 1,300 meters.

"We were not expecting to find a new species," said Dr. Halina Brzezicka, an ecologist at the Greystone Institute for Natural Sciences and lead author of the study. "We were there to carry out a routine survey of invertebrates as part of a long-term monitoring project. When we started sorting the samples, a few of the specimens simply did not match anything in the reference collections."

To confirm their suspicion, the team compared the beetles' physical features, including the structure of the male reproductive organs, which entomologists often use to distinguish closely related species, with those of known relatives. They also sequenced a standard section of the beetles' DNA. Both lines of evidence indicated that the population represented a distinct species, most closely related to a beetle found in mountain ranges several hundred kilometers to the south.

The researchers believe the new species may have become isolated at the end of the last ice age, when warming temperatures pushed cold-adapted insects upslope and divided once-connected populations onto separate mountain tops.

Ground beetles of this kind are predators, feeding mainly on snails, slugs, and other small invertebrates. They are active mostly at night and spend daylight hours sheltering beneath stones. Their presence can be a useful indicator of the health of an ecosystem.

The study's authors caution that the species may be vulnerable. Over a two-year survey, they recorded fewer than sixty individuals, all within an area of about four square kilometers. Because the beetle cannot fly and appears to depend on cool, damp conditions, rising temperatures could reduce its habitat further.

"When a species exists only on the upper slopes of a few mountains, it has nowhere higher to go," Brzezicka said. "That makes it a kind of early warning for changes in the whole alpine environment."

The reserve's management authority welcomed the discovery. A spokesperson said the area where the beetle was found already lies within a protected zone where off-trail access is restricted, but that the authority would review whether additional measures were needed, such as moving a section of hiking trail that passes close to the boulder fields.

The research team plans to return next summer to map the beetle's range in more detail and to study its life cycle, about which almost nothing is yet known.

"Every new species is a reminder of how much we still have to learn, even in places we think we know well," Brzezicka said. "This reserve has been visited by naturalists for more than a century, and this beetle was there the whole time, quietly living under the rocks."

I started learning Japanese at forty-three, which is roughly thirty years after the age at which, according to everything I had read, the brain begins to close its doors to new languages. I knew this when I began. I began anyway, partly out of stubbornness and partly because I had promised myself, years earlier, that I would someday be able to order a bowl of noodles in Osaka without pointing.

The first months were humbling in a way I had not experienced since childhood. I am used to being competent. My job involves explaining complicated things to people, and I am reasonably good at it. Suddenly I was someone who could not reliably tell the difference between two characters that, to my untrained eye, consisted of the same three strokes in slightly different moods. I would study a list of words in the evening and find, the next morning, that it had been wiped clean overnight like a whiteboard.

What surprised me was not the difficulty but how much I came to enjoy the feeling of being a beginner. There is a particular kind of freedom in being bad at something on purpose. Nobody expects much of you. Every small success, such as reading a station name on a photograph or catching a single sentence in a film without the subtitles, feels enormous out of all proportion to its real size.

I also discovered that adult learners have advantages that the gloomy articles do not mention. I know how I learn. I know that I remember things better if I write them by hand, that I need to say new words out loud, and that I will abandon any system that requires more than thirty minutes a day. A child does not know these things.
